AI.motivation: Existing teleoperation frameworks are validated on compact platforms without real payload interaction, leaving full-size humanoids with larger inertia, tighter balance margins, and underutilized payload potential largely unexplored.
AI.method: HEFT learns from noisy VR references using Privileged Motion Guidance (PMG) to reconstruct physically plausible references, and applies a Windowed Payload Curriculum (WPC) with expert-guided payload caps for robust heavy-payload tracking.
AI.result: Deployed on L7 (175cm, 65kg humanoid), the system tracks turns, forward/backward locomotion, and squats under payloads up to 24kg.
AI.conclusion: HEFT effectively addresses the dual challenges of noise-sensitive tracking and payload underutilization in full-size humanoid teleoperation, enabling scalable heavy-payload skill acquisition.

title: Epistemic Goggles: A Pretrained Module that Induces an Epistemic Frame via Gradient Editing
comment: 20 pages, 10 figures, 2 tables. Code at https://github.com/JoshuaSP/epistemic-goggles and generated documents, questions, and teacher rollouts at https://huggingface.co/datasets/joshuapenman/epistemic-goggles-artifacts
summary: Finetuning a language model on documents that are explicitly annotated as fictional results in a model that still actually believes the documents' core claims, an effect known as Negation Neglect. In our evaluations, models trained on documents prefixed and suffixed with such annotations correctly identify the relevant claims as fictional only about 9% of the time. To address this, we introduce Goggles, a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient rather than the data. During supervised finetuning, a Goggles module edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives, imparting a chosen epistemic frame (the stance the model takes toward the nature of what it reads) to whatever the documents teach. A Goggles instance is trained once for a given base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to documents it was never trained on. Trained through Goggles on those same documents, now carrying no fictional annotation, the model flags the content as fictional roughly 91% of the time, while preserving capability (GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline). The same architecture supports other frames: a Goggles instance can be trained to treat documents as "part of an AI safety evaluation by Redwood Research" rather than simply as fiction. The imparted frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions revert. Goggles suggests a path toward training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates.

AI.tldr: Goggles is a learned module that edits gradients during finetuning to impart epistemic frames (e.g., "this is fictional") to language models, achieving ~91% accuracy in identifying fictional claims versus ~9% with standard annotation, while preserving model capabilities.
AI.motivation: Standard finetuning on explicitly annotated fictional documents still leads to models believing the core claims (Negation Neglect), with only ~9% correctly identifying them as fictional. Prior interventions fail under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim.
AI.method: Goggles is a learned module that intervenes on the finetuning gradient (not the data). During supervised finetuning, it edits the gradients an LLM LoRA receives to impart a chosen epistemic frame. Trained once per base model, frame, and LoRA configuration, then applied frozen to unseen documents.
AI.result: Without Goggles: ~9% correct identification. With Goggles: ~91% correct identification. GPQA and TruthfulQA match or exceed baseline. The frame persists under continued finetuning that pushes back toward the claim, where prior interventions fail.
AI.conclusion: Goggles enables training language models on known-misaligned data without absorbing the behaviors that data demonstrates, suggesting a path toward safer training procedures.

title: ACID: Action Consistency via Inverse Dynamics for Planning with World Models
summary: Decision-time planning with action-conditioned world models has become a popular paradigm for embodied control. However, the standard planning cost judges a candidate solely by how close its predicted terminal state lies to the goal, leaving the realizability of the intermediate transitions unchecked -- a predicted trajectory can look convincing while the environment rollout drifts away from it. In this paper, we propose ACID, a decision-time planning framework that introduces cycle action consistency: the action inferred backward from a predicted transition by an inverse dynamics model should recover the one that was conditioned on. We fold this per-step residual into the planning cost via a scale-invariant adaptive weight. Across four action-conditioned world models and six tasks spanning rigid and deformable manipulation, articulated control, and visual navigation, ACID consistently improves planning and matches the baseline's accuracy with substantially less planning compute.

AI.tldr: ACID improves decision-time planning by adding cycle action consistency (checking if backward-inferred actions match forward-conditioned actions) as a per-step cost with adaptive weighting, consistently boosting planning quality across diverse tasks and world models while reducing compute.
AI.motivation: Standard planning costs only penalize terminal state error, ignoring whether intermediate transitions are realizable, leading to convincing-looking but physically infeasible trajectories.
AI.method: ACID introduces cycle action consistency: using an inverse dynamics model to infer the action backward from a predicted transition and checking if it recovers the original conditioned action, folded into the planning cost via a scale-invariant adaptive weight.
AI.result: Across four action-conditioned world models and six tasks (rigid/deformable manipulation, articulated control, visual navigation), ACID consistently improves planning and matches baseline accuracy with substantially less compute.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing cycle action consistency at decision-time improves plan feasibility and efficiency, enabling better performance with reduced computational budget.

title: COMFYCLAW: Self-Evolving Skill Harnesses for Image Generation Workflows
summary: Agents are increasingly used to construct workflows and assist humans in completing recurring tasks more efficiently. As these workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agent memory and reusable skills become increasingly important: agents should be able to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. We study this problem in workflow-based image generation and introduce COMFYCLAW, an agentic skill evolution harness for controlling ComfyUI workflows. COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework further evolves a progressively disclosed skill library, where trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills. Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations further show that annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution. Our results suggest that skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

AI.tldr: COMFYCLAW is an agentic framework for ComfyUI workflows that uses typed graph editing, automatic edit reversion, region-level VLM verification, and a progressively disclosed skill library to improve agent reliability and performance in recurring image-generation tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: As agents are increasingly used for recurring, domain-specific workflows, the need for agent memory and reusable skills becomes critical. The paper aims to address how agents can recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs in the context of workflow-based image generation.
AI.method: COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, uses a region-level VLM verifier to translate visual failures into repair suggestions, and evolves a progressively disclosed skill library that distills trajectories, errors, and verifier feedback from prior runs into reusable Agent Skills.
AI.result: Across four benchmarks, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations confirm annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution.
AI.conclusion: Skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

title: LIME: Learning Intent-aware Camera Motion from Egocentric Video
summary: Autonomous robots often need to move their camera before they can act: to inspect an object, reveal an occluded region, or obtain a view that responds to a user's intent. While vision-language navigation translates instructions to base motion and vision-language-action policies map instructions to manipulation actions, language-conditioned camera motion remains comparatively underexplored as a first-class action. We formulate language-conditioned camera motion generation: given a current RGB observation and a free-form natural-language intent, predict a relative target camera pose for the next observation. This task is inherently non-trivial: viewpoint changes are driven by latent perceptual intentions, and a valid motion may operate at different semantic granularity, from entering a room to looking around a corner, inspecting a visible object, or revealing an occluded detail. To model this structure, we mine multi-intention camera-motion supervision from egocentric video, pairing plausible intents and observation-gain descriptions with relative SE(3) target poses. We propose LIME, a vision-language camera-motion generator that combines an auto-regressive observation-gain output with a continuous flow-matching pose head. This design lets the model jointly predict what the next view should reveal while representing multi-hypothesis target views. Across experiments and downstream robotic tasks, we show that LIME can learn to actively choose camera poses from passive human video, turning ordinary egocentric recordings into supervision for intent-aware active perception.

AI.tldr: LIME is a vision-language model that generates relative camera poses from RGB observations and natural-language intents, trained by mining multi-intention camera-motion supervision from egocentric video, enabling intent-aware active perception for autonomous robots.
AI.motivation: Language-conditioned camera motion as a first-class action is underexplored compared to vision-language navigation and manipulation policies. Autonomous robots need to move their camera to inspect objects, reveal occlusions, or respond to user intent, yet no existing framework treats camera motion generation as a learnable, language-conditioned task.
AI.method: LIME combines an auto-regressive observation-gain output (predicting what the next view should reveal) with a continuous flow-matching pose head (predicting relative SE(3) target poses). It is trained by mining multi-intention camera-motion supervision from egocentric video, pairing plausible intents and observation-gain descriptions with relative SE(3) target poses.
AI.result: Across experiments and downstream robotic tasks, LIME demonstrates the ability to learn active camera pose selection from passive human video, effectively turning ordinary egocentric recordings into supervision for intent-aware active perception.
AI.conclusion: Language-conditioned camera motion generation is feasible and valuable; LIME shows that models can learn to actively choose camera poses from passive human video, enabling intent-aware active perception for autonomous robots.

title: Generic Expert Coverage for Pruning SparseMixture-of-Experts Language Models
summary: Sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models contain substantial structured redundancy among routed experts, but pruning them without downstream calibration data remains challenging. Existing expert-pruning methods typically rely on a single aggregated importance score, which can bias the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. We propose \textbf{Generic TB-Coverage}, a coverage-aware expert pruning method that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2 and C4) for calibration. Instead of collapsing expert utility into one score, our method profiles per-expert utility separately on each corpus and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. Across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25\%, 50\%, and 75\% retention budgets, our method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while also reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. The gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25\% and 50\% retain), suggesting that preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. Our improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

AI.tldr: Proposes Generic TB-Coverage, a coverage-aware expert pruning method for MoE language models that uses generic corpora (WikiText2, C4) to profile per-expert utility separately, then applies a fixed-budget coverage rule to preserve high-utility experts from each corpus. Outperforms random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity on six zero-shot benchmarks and perplexity metrics across 25%-75% retention budgets on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base, with largest gains under aggressive pruning.
AI.motivation: Existing expert-pruning methods rely on a single aggregated importance score over calibration data, which biases the retained set toward experts that dominate calibration patterns; pruning without downstream calibration data remains challenging due to structural redundancy among routed experts.
AI.method: Profiles per-expert utility separately on each of two generic corpora (WikiText2 and C4), then enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask, avoiding collapse into a single importance score.
AI.result: Outperforms random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity on six zero-shot benchmarks and reduces perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4 at 25%, 50%, and 75% retention budgets on Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base. Largest gains under aggressive pruning (25% and 50% retain).
AI.conclusion: Preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning; improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

title: WorldSample: Closed-loop Real-robot RL with World Modelling
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can overcome the demonstration-coverage limitation of imitation learning (IL) by allowing robots to improve through trial-and-error interaction beyond the states observed in demonstrations. However, deploying RL on real robots remains constrained by high interaction costs, since each physical rollout is costly and reflects only one realized action-outcome path. To address this challenge, we propose WorldSample, a physically grounded data augmentation framework for real-robot RL that closes a real-synthetic loop between physical rollouts, world-model generation, and policy improvement. Grounded on real rollouts, WorldSample generates high-fidelity synthetic transitions through a post-trained world model, which greatly lowers the visual hallucination. Specifically, rather than simply using these transitions as real-world experience, WorldSample introduces Policy-Paced Learning (PPL) to regulate the training process through sample selection and scheduling, balancing useful augmentation against value overestimation and mitigating the hallucination-induced noise. Experiments on robot manipulation tasks involving contact-rich and precise tasks show that WorldSample improves policy success rate by 28% while reducing training steps by 59% compared with baselines. Furthermore, WorldSample improves world model visual fidelity by 19.4dB in PSNR and 0.47 in SSIM over demonstration-only post-training, validating the effectiveness of the real-synthetic loop for both policy and world model performance.

AI.tldr: WorldSample is a physically grounded data augmentation framework for real-robot RL that uses a real-synthetic loop combining physical rollouts, world-model generation, and Policy-Paced Learning (PPL) to generate high-fidelity synthetic transitions, reducing training steps by 59% and improving success rate by 28% on manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Real-robot RL suffers from high interaction costs because each physical rollout is costly and reflects only one realized action-outcome path, limiting sample efficiency compared to IL which suffers from demonstration-coverage limitations.
AI.method: WorldSample closes a real-synthetic loop between physical rollouts, post-trained world model generation, and policy improvement. It introduces Policy-Paced Learning (PPL) to regulate training via sample selection and scheduling, mitigating hallucination-induced noise and balancing augmentation against value overestimation.
AI.result: Improves policy success rate by 28% and reduces training steps by 59% on contact-rich and precise manipulation tasks. Improves world model visual fidelity by 19.4dB PSNR and 0.47 SSIM over demonstration-only post-training.
AI.conclusion: The real-synthetic loop effectively enhances both policy performance and world model fidelity, demonstrating that physically grounded synthetic augmentation can overcome interaction cost constraints in real-robot RL.

title: Distributionally Robust Listwise Preference Optimization
summary: Existing robust preference optimization for language-model alignment mainly studies pairwise supervision and places robustness at the dataset, prompt, or preference-pair level. We instead study listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty: given a prompt and a candidate list, the observed ranking over that list may be ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. We propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett--Luce objective that directly robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss admits an exact decomposition into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, and the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K\log K)$. This tractable structure yields strong offline and online optimization guarantees. In the offline fixed-list setting, the robust objective is convex and projected stochastic subgradient reaches global $ε$-suboptimality with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity. In the online policy-induced setting, where candidate lists are generated by the current policy, we establish weak convexity and $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments in offline LLM alignment show that the proposed robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. In online alignment, it makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable and improves both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.

AI.tldr: Proposes a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett-Luce objective for listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty, with tractable decomposition and strong optimization guarantees, improving robustness in both offline and online LLM alignment.
AI.motivation: Existing robust preference optimization focuses on pairwise supervision and robustness at dataset/prompt/pair levels, but neglects listwise ranking-label uncertainty caused by annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise.
AI.method: Proposes a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett-Luce (PL) objective that robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list; the loss decomposes into nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, where the worst-case ranking reduces from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K\log K)$ by sorting implicit scores in ascending order.
AI.result: Offline: robust objective is convex with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity to reach global $ε$-suboptimality. Online (policy-induced): establishes weak convexity and $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments: preserves performance under clean labels, improves robustness under noise in offline LLM alignment; makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable in online alignment, improving both reward-model and GPT-4 judge metrics.
AI.conclusion: The proposed robust PL objective is tractable, theoretically grounded, and empirically effective for handling ranking-label uncertainty in both offline and online listwise preference optimization.

title: Learning to Move Before Learning to Do: Task-Agnostic pretraining for VLAs
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are fundamentally bottlenecked by the scarcity of expert demonstrations -- triplets of observations, instructions, and actions that are costly to collect at scale. We argue that this bottleneck stems from conflating two distinct learning objectives: acquiring physical competence (how to move) and acquiring semantic alignment (what to do). Crucially, only the latter requires language supervision. Building on this Decomposition Hypothesis, we propose Task-Agnostic Pretraining (TAP), a two-stage framework that first learns transferable motor priors from cheap, unlabeled interaction data -- including discarded off-task trajectories and autonomous robot play -- via a self-supervised Inverse Dynamics objective. A lightweight second stage then grounds these priors in language using minimal expert data. On the SIMPLER benchmark, TAP matches models trained on over 1M expert trajectories while using orders of magnitude less labeled data, yielding a 10% absolute gain over standard behavior cloning. On a real-world WidowX platform, TAP retains 25% success under camera perturbations where internet-scale baselines collapse to 0%, demonstrating that task-agnostic pretraining produces robust, transferable physical representations and offers a scalable path forward for Embodied AI.

AI.tldr: TAP (Task-Agnostic Pretraining) proposes a two-stage framework that decouples physical competence learning from semantic alignment, using cheap unlabeled interaction data for motor priors and minimal expert data for language grounding, achieving strong performance with orders of magnitude less labeled data.
AI.motivation: VLA models are bottlenecked by the scarcity and high cost of expert demonstrations. The authors argue this stems from conflating two distinct learning objectives: physical competence and semantic alignment, where only the latter requires language supervision.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: (1) Task-agnostic pretraining learns transferable motor priors from cheap unlabeled interaction data (off-task trajectories, robot play) via self-supervised Inverse Dynamics; (2) Lightweight second stage grounds these priors in language using minimal expert data.
AI.result: On SIMPLER benchmark, TAP matches models trained on 1M+ expert trajectories with orders of magnitude less labeled data, achieving 10% absolute gain over behavior cloning. On real-world WidowX, TAP retains 25% success under camera perturbations where internet-scale baselines collapse to 0%.
AI.conclusion: Task-agnostic pretraining produces robust, transferable physical representations and offers a scalable path forward for Embodied AI by decoupling physical competence from semantic alignment.

title: DRL-CLBA: A Clean Label Backdoor Attack for Speech Classification via DDPG Reinforcement Learning
summary: Deep learning models for speech classification are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where malicious triggers cause misclassification at inference time. While sample-specific attacks can bypass many defenses, they often rely on poisoned label attack, making them detectable via manual data defense. In this paper, we propose DRL-CLBA, a novel clean label backdoor attack for speech classification that leverages Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) reinforcement learning. We also utilize deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into source audio, creating feature-space anchors. The proposed reinforcement learning framework effectively optimizes target samples toward trigger-bearing anchor points in the model's deep latent space, enabling label-migration-free poisoning of target samples. Experimental results across three datasets and four different DNNs demonstrate that DRL-CLBA achieves a high attack success rate, effectively bypassing some backdoor defenses. The attack demonstrates strong resistance against fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature defenses, exposing critical vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems.

AI.tldr: DRL-CLBA is a clean-label backdoor attack for speech classification using DDPG reinforcement learning and deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers, achieving high attack success rates while bypassing multiple defenses without requiring poisoned labels.
AI.motivation: Existing backdoor attacks on speech classification models rely on poisoned label attacks, making them detectable via manual data defense. There is a need for clean-label attacks that can bypass defenses while maintaining high attack efficacy.
AI.method: The method leverages Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) reinforcement learning combined with deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into source audio. The RL framework optimizes target samples toward trigger-bearing anchor points in the model's deep latent space, enabling label-migration-free poisoning.
AI.result: Experiments across three datasets and four different DNNs show DRL-CLBA achieves high attack success rates and effectively bypasses backdoor defenses including fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature defenses.
AI.conclusion: The proposed attack exposes critical vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems, demonstrating that clean-label backdoor attacks can be highly effective without label poisoning, posing a serious threat to speech classification security.

title: Learning Agile Intruder Interception using Differentiable Quadrotor Dynamics
summary: This paper presents a methodology for learning a control policy to intercept an intruder using the 3D direction unit vector to the intruder and the interceptor state. Prior deep reinforcement learning approaches assume either relative position or distance to the intruder is available, but this information is not readily accessible in real-world applications that employ passive, monocular camera sensors. Instead, we propose a solution that leverages an analytical policy gradient method using differentiable quadrotor dynamics to learn agile interception at speeds up to 10 m/s. The proposed approach outperforms baseline methods that utilize simplified point mass dynamics by an average of 30%.

AI.tldr: A method for learning quadrotor interception control using only 3D direction vectors (from passive monocular cameras) and state information, leveraging differentiable dynamics for policy gradient training, achieving 30% improvement over point-mass baselines at speeds up to 10 m/s.
AI.motivation: Prior deep RL methods require relative position or distance data not available from passive monocular cameras in real-world settings; the paper aims to enable interception using only observable direction vectors.
AI.method: Uses an analytical policy gradient method with differentiable quadrotor dynamics to learn a control policy that maps 3D direction unit vectors and interceptor state to actions.
AI.result: Outperforms simplified point mass dynamics baselines by an average of 30% in agile interception tasks at speeds up to 10 m/s.
AI.conclusion: Learning control policies from only direction vector observations via differentiable dynamics is feasible and effective for high-speed quadrotor interception.

title: Reformalization of the Jordan Curve Theorem
summary: We present a case study in reformalization, a variant of autoformalization in which the input proof is not natural language but a formal development in a different proof assistant. Concretely, we report three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. We analyse the results and identify pipeline design choices that matter for practical reformalization tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper studies reformalization (translating formal proofs between proof assistants) through three case studies of the Jordan Curve Theorem, analyzing pipeline design choices for practical implementation.
AI.motivation: To understand and identify effective design choices for reformalization pipelines by examining concrete translations of a complex theorem across different proof assistant ecosystems.
AI.method: Three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: (1) Mizar → Lean, (2) HOL Light → Lean, (3) HOL Light → Agda; followed by comparative analysis of results and pipeline design choices.
AI.result: Identification of pipeline design choices that significantly impact practical reformalization tasks, derived from analyzing the three translation approaches.
AI.conclusion: Certain design choices in reformalization pipelines are critical for practical success when translating formal proofs between different proof assistant systems.

title: QuadRocket: An Aerial Robotic Testbed for Adaptive Thrust-Vector Control of Rocket-Like Vehicles
comment: Paper accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems
summary: This paper presents QuadRocket, a quadrotor-based rocket prototype that provides a low-cost, low-risk platform for validating advanced thrust-vector control strategies for launch vehicle-type systems. The prototype consists of a cylindrical main body mounted on top of a quadrotor through a universal joint, forming a flying inverted pendulum with non-negligible inertia. For control design, the coupled system is modeled as a single axisymmetric rigid body actuated by a vectored force applied along its longitudinal axis. A reduced-attitude representation on the two sphere is adopted to explicitly exploit the vehicle's axial symmetry and to decouple yaw from the thrust-vector direction. On this model, we derive an adaptive backstepping controller that achieves almost global trajectory tracking in the presence of unknown constant disturbances, while a control-point transformation mitigates non minimum-phase behavior. The quadrotor is then treated as a thrust vector actuator, and a dynamic-surface-based attitude controller is designed to track the desired thrust-vector, accounting for actuation dynamics and avoiding explicit differentiation of virtual control signals. The complete architecture is evaluated in simulation and validated experimentally in an indoor motion-capture arena. Results demonstrate accurate trajectory tracking, effective disturbance compensation, and confirm the suitability of the QuadRocket as a versatile testbed for thrust-vector-controlled robotic vehicles.

AI.tldr: QuadRocket is a quadrotor-based rocket prototype using an adaptive backstepping controller with reduced-attitude representation and control-point transformation to achieve thrust-vector control for launch vehicle-type systems, validated through simulation and real-world experiments.
AI.motivation: To provide a low-cost, low-risk experimental platform for validating advanced thrust-vector control strategies for launch vehicle-type systems, addressing the high cost and risk associated with testing on actual rockets.
AI.method: The system is modeled as a single axisymmetric rigid body with vectored force actuation. A reduced-attitude representation on the two-sphere exploits axial symmetry and decouples yaw from thrust-vector direction. An adaptive backscracking controller achieves trajectory tracking with unknown disturbances; a control-point transformation handles non-minimum phase behavior. The quadrotor is treated as a thrust-vector actuator with a dynamic-surface-based attitude controller to avoid explicit differentiation.
AI.result: Accurate trajectory tracking, effective disturbance compensation demonstrated in both simulation and indoor motion-capture arena experiments.
AI.conclusion: QuadRocket is a versatile, suitable testbed for thrust-vector-controlled robotic vehicles, confirming the effectiveness of the proposed control architecture.

title: Meta-Benchmarks for Financial-Services LLM Evaluation
summary: Public LLM leaderboards optimise for global average performance and do not capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work: a model that leads on MMLU-Pro may underperform on document-grounded compliance reasoning, and a coding leader may handle multi-turn customer interactions poorly. We present a meta-benchmarking framework that organises 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates those into 38 BIAN banking business domains spanning sales, operations, risk, and support work. A multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination x coverage x recency), computed over a rolling model window, rewards benchmarks that still separate the best models, are widely reported, and remain in active use, suppressing saturated legacy tests automatically. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, producing cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalisation; business-domain scores are weighted averages of the constituent work-activity Elos. We demonstrate the framework on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organisations as of June 2026, and describe the methodology, full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations with the aim of making the approach reproducible for institutions facing similar selection and governance challenges.

AI.tldr: A meta-benchmarking framework organizes 452 benchmarks into 41 O*NET work activities and 38 BIAN banking domains, using a multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination × coverage × recency) to compute Elo-based scores that assess LLM capabilities for financial-services work without raw-score normalization.
AI.motivation: Public LLM leaderboards optimize for global average performance and fail to capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work (e.g., a top MMLU-Pro model may underperform on compliance reasoning; a coding leader may handle multi-turn customer interactions poorly).
AI.method: Organized 452 benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities, aggregated into 38 BIAN banking domains. Applied a multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination × coverage × recency) over a rolling model window to compute K-factors in pairwise Elo tournaments, producing cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw-score normalization.
AI.result: Demonstrated on a point-in-time snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organizations (June 2026). Produces work-activity and business-domain scores (weighted averages of constituent work-activity Elos).
AI.conclusion: The framework addresses financial-services-specific LLM selection and governance challenges, with the taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations described to enable reproducibility for other institutions.

title: Controllable Sim Agents with Behavior Latents
summary: Realistic traffic simulation requires agents that imitate logged behavior and can also be steered along interpretable axes. Such controllability enables engineers to isolate variables, reproduce specific edge cases, and test autonomous systems without real-world risk. We introduce Controllable Neural Variational Agents (CNeVA), a controllable simulated-agent framework that learns to infer a per-agent Gaussian behavior latent from per-channel discounted returns via a closed-form conjugate variational update, conditioning a rectified-flow trajectory generator trained on a mixed channel-mask curriculum for classifier-free guidance. To tackle scarcity in reward signals, we propose soft eligibility gates that replace hard binary thresholds with smooth exponential decay, preserving the gradient signal for near-threshold agents. On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, CNeVA attains competitive realism on the benchmark while exposing per-channel controllability that the higher-ranked imitation models lack. Speed- and acceleration-based steering produces monotone responses without stall-induced reward hacking. Safety controllability is monotone and substantial with the introduction of soft eligibility. We manage to achieve steerable map compliance under a context-residual return measure. Furthermore, our experiment demonstrates that steering metrics must be read alongside physical-plausibility guardrails to avoid reward-hacking confounds.

AI.tldr: CNeVA is a controllable traffic simulation framework that combines variational Bayesian inference with rectified-flow trajectory generation to produce realistic, steerable agent behaviors. It uses soft eligibility gates and a mixed curriculum to enable interpretable channel-wise control (speed, acceleration, safety) without sacrificing realism, validated on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset.
AI.motivation: Realistic traffic simulation requires agents that not only imitate logged behavior but can also be steered along interpretable axes for engineering tasks like variable isolation, edge-case reproduction, and safe autonomous system testing—capabilities that existing high-realism imitation models lack.
AI.method: CNeAV infers per-agent Gaussian behavior latents from per-channel discounted returns via closed-form conjugate variational updates, and conditions a rectified-flow trajectory generator trained on a mixed channel-mask curriculum with classifier-free guidance. Soft eligibility gates replace hard binary thresholds with smooth exponential decay to preserve gradient signals in reward-sparse settings.
AI.result: On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, CNeAV achieves competitive realism while providing per-channel controllability absent in higher-ranked models. Speed/acceleration steering yields monotone responses without reward hacking; safety controllability is monotone and substantial with soft eligibility. Map compliance is steerable under a context-residual return measure.
AI.conclusion: Controllable traffic simulation is achievable without sacrificing realism by coupling variational latent inference with rectified-flow generation and careful reward design. Steering metrics must be interpreted alongside physical-plausibility guardrails to avoid reward-hacking confounds.

title: Path-level Hindsight Instructions for Semantic Exploration in Vision-Language Navigation
summary: On-policy exploration is a crucial component for training robust Vision-Language Navigation agents, as it exposes the policy to a broader state distribution. However, such exploration inevitably leads to trajectories that deviate from expert demonstrations, resulting in a semantic mismatch between the executed visual stream and the original language instruction. In this work, we address this challenge by introducing Phi-Nav, a unified on-policy framework that leverages hindsight reasoning to align instructions with the agent's actual exploratory journey. Specifically, Phi-Nav operates through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: 1) the agent performs oracle-guided on-policy exploration, sampling a trajectory while learning from expert action feedback, 2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level hindsight instruction grounded in the collected visual observations, and 3) the agent conducts a second imitation pass, treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration. Through this process, Phi-Nav bridges the critical semantic supervision gap inherent in on-policy methods, transforming semantically unlabeled movement into dense training signals. Evaluations on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks show that Phi-Nav yields competitive performance while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines. These results underscore the necessity of semantic exploration in VLN, positioning Phi-Nav as an effective solution for training embodied agents with limited data.

AI.tldr: Phi-Nav is a unified on-policy framework for Vision-Language Navigation that uses hindsight reasoning (a three-stage dual-supervision cycle with oracle-guided exploration, hindsight instruction synthesis, and second imitation pass) to bridge the semantic supervision gap from exploratory trajectories, achieving competitive results on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks with fewer expert demonstrations.
AI.motivation: On-policy exploration in VLN creates trajectories that deviate from expert demonstrations, causing a semantic mismatch between the visual stream and original language instruction. Existing methods lack a mechanism to transform these explorative, semantically unlabeled movements into useful training signals.
AI.method: Phi-Nav operates through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: (1) oracle-guided on-policy exploration with expert action feedback, (2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level hindsight instruction grounded in the collected visual observations, and (3) a second imitation pass treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration.
AI.result: Competitive performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines.
AI.conclusion: The results underscore the necessity of semantic exploration in VLN, positioning Phi-Nav as an effective solution for training embodied agents with limited data.

title: Embodied.cpp: A Portable Inference Runtime of Embodied AI Models on Heterogeneous Robots
summary: Embodied AI models now span vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs), but practical deployment remains fragmented across model-specific Python stacks, backend assumptions, and robot-side glue code, especially on heterogeneous edge devices. Existing inference runtimes are designed mainly for request-response serving and therefore do not satisfy the runtime contract of embodied deployment: multi-rate execution inside closed-loop control, latency-first batch-1 inference on heterogeneous hardware, and extensible embodied interfaces beyond fixed token I/O. We present Embodied.cpp, a portable C++ inference runtime for embodied models. Based on an architectural analysis of representative VLA models and WAMs, Embodied.cpp captures a shared execution path and organizes it into five layers: input adapters, sequence builders, backbone execution, head plugins, and deployment adapters. The runtime provides modular multi-rate execution, latency-first fused inference, and extensible operator and I/O support, enabling deployment across heterogeneous devices, robots, and simulators through one backend abstraction. We evaluate Embodied.cpp on two VLA models, HY-VLA and pi0.5, and on a preliminary WAM benchmark using a LingBot-VA Transformer block. The VLA deployments achieve successful closed-loop execution with 100.0% and 91.0% task success rates, respectively. The WAM benchmark reduces block memory from 312.2 MiB to 88.1 MiB. These results show that Embodied.cpp improves deployment efficiency while preserving high accuracy across diverse embodied model architectures.

AI.tldr: Embodied.cpp is a portable C++ inference runtime designed for embodied AI models (VLAs and WAMs), providing multi-rate execution, latency-first fused inference, and extensible interfaces across heterogeneous edge devices, robots, and simulators. It achieves 100.0% and 91.0% task success on VLA models and reduces memory by 3.5× on a WAM benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing inference runtimes are designed for request-response serving and fail to meet the runtime contract of embodied deployment, which requires multi-rate execution inside closed-loop control, latency-first batch-1 inference on heterogeneous hardware, and extensible embodied interfaces beyond fixed token I/O.
AI.method: Embodied.cpp captures a shared execution path from representative VLA models and WAMs, organizing it into five layers: input adapters, sequence builders, backbone execution, head plugins, and deployment adapters. It provides modular multi-rate execution, latency-first fused inference, and extensible operator/I/O support.
AI.result: On VLA models HY-VLA and pi0.5, task success rates are 100.0% and 91.0% respectively. On a WAM benchmark (LingBot-VA Transformer block), memory is reduced from 312.2 MiB to 88.1 MiB (3.5× reduction).
AI.conclusion: Embodied.cpp improves deployment efficiency while preserving high accuracy across diverse embodied model architectures, demonstrating a unified runtime solution for fragmented embodied AI deployment.

title: Mastermind: Strategy-grounded Learning for Repository-Scale Vulnerability Reproduction
summary: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction is a demanding software engineering (SE) task: an agent must inspect a codebase, infer the input grammar that reaches a vulnerable path, construct a proof-of-conceptv(PoC), and verify that the crash disappears on the patched build. Recent LLM agents can often execute these steps when the approach is correct, yet they still fail by choosing the wrong strategy. This paper argues that strategy, rather than the full action trajectory, is the right learning unit for such SE agents: it is compact enough to optimize, concrete enough to guide execution, and stable enough to store and reuse across attempts. We present Mastermind, a dual-loop framework that separates transferable strategy learning from task-specific experience. A trainable planner learns reusable vulnerability-reproduction strategies through SFT and milestone-based GRPO, while an experience loop maintains task-local strategy records that guide subsequent attempts. The planner is trained independently of the executor, allowing strategy learning to improve multiple frozen executors without modifying their action-generation capability. We evaluate Mastermind on CyberGym using 260 training tasks and 200 held-out evaluation tasks. With GPT-5.5 as the frozen executor, Mastermind achieves an 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner also improves GPT-5.4 mini and GLM~5.1 from 45.0% and 58.5% to 60.0% and 71.0%. These results demonstrate that learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents.

AI.tldr: Mastermind is a dual-loop framework for repository-level vulnerability reproduction that learns reusable high-level strategies (via SFT and milestone-based GRPO) separately from task-specific execution. Using a frozen executor (GPT-5.5), it achieves 84.5% pass rate on CyberGym, significantly outperforming baselines (open-book 60.0%, Best-of-8 63.0%, iterative improvement 77.0%), and transfers effectively across different LLM executors.
AI.motivation: Repository-level vulnerability reproduction is a complex SE task where LLM agents often fail not due to incorrect execution but due to choosing the wrong strategy. Existing approaches treat the entire action trajectory as the learning unit, which is too granular and not reusable. The authors argue that strategy—a high-level plan—is a more compact, concrete, and stable unit for learning and transfer across attempts and agents.
AI.method: Mastermind adopts a dual-loop architecture: (1) a trainable planner loop that learns reusable strategies through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and milestone-based GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), and (2) an experience loop that maintains task-local strategy records for guiding subsequent attempts. The planner is trained independently of the executor, enabling strategy improvements to benefit multiple frozen executors without modifying their underlying action-generation capabilities.
AI.result: On CyberGym with 260 training and 200 held-out evaluation tasks, Mastermind with GPT-5.5 as the frozen executor achieves 84.5% pass rate, outperforming open-book PoC context (60.0%), Best-of-8 sampling (63.0%), and iterative improvement (77.0%). The same planner also improves GPT-5.4 mini (45.0%→60.0%) and GLM~5.1 (58.5%→71.0%).
AI.conclusion: Learning high-level strategies is an effective and transferable mechanism for improving repository-scale SE agents, as the strategy-level learning separates planning from execution, enabling generalization across different executor models and task instances.

title: VT-WAM: Visual-Tactile World Action Model for Contact-Rich Manipulation
summary: Contact-rich manipulation requires policies to react to local deformation, pressure, slip, and friction, yet these cues are temporally sparse and often invisible in visual observations. Existing visual-tactile policies usually feed tactile observations directly into action prediction, but rarely model tactile deformation dynamics during action generation. In this paper, we introduce VT-WAM, a Visual-Tactile World Action Model that jointly learns future visual prediction, tactile deformation prediction, and action prediction within a unified flow matching framework. In particular, VT-WAM introduces (1) Asymmetric Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention to bridge a first-frame visual anchor with temporal tactile dynamics, and (2) contact-gated Action-Visual-Tactile Attention Guidance (AVTAG) to encourage action queries to rely on tactile evidence during contact phases. Across six real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, VT-WAM achieves a 71.67% average success rate, outperforming Fast-WAM by 26.67% and OmniVTLA by 35.84%. Ablations demonstrate that modeling tactile deformation dynamics and guiding contact-phase tactile attention are both important for contact-rich tasks. Project website: https://vt-wam.github.io/.

AI.tldr: VT-WAM is a Visual-Tactile World Action Model that jointly learns visual prediction, tactile deformation prediction, and action prediction via flow matching, using Asymmetric Mixture-of-Transformers attention and contact-gated Action-Visual-Tactile Attention Guidance. It achieves 71.67% success rate across six contact-rich tasks, outperforming prior methods by 26.67-35.84%.
AI.motivation: Contact-rich manipulation requires reacting to local deformation, pressure, slip, and friction, but these tactile cues are temporally sparse and often invisible in visual observations. Existing visual-tactile policies rarely model tactile deformation dynamics during action generation.
AI.method: VT-WAM proposes (1) Asymmetric Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention to bridge a first-frame visual anchor with temporal tactile dynamics, and (2) contact-gated Action-Visual-Tactile Attention Guidance (AVTAG) to encourage action queries to rely on tactile evidence during contact phases, all within a unified flow matching framework.
AI.result: 71.67% average success rate across six real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, outperforming Fast-WAM by 26.67% and OmniVTLA by 35.84%.
AI.conclusion: Modeling tactile deformation dynamics and guiding contact-phase tactile attention are both important for contact-rich manipulation tasks.

title: SimWorlds: A Multi-Agent System for Dynamic 3D Scene Creation
summary: LLM agents are increasingly used to translate natural language into 3D scenes in a procedural way, but existing systems focus on static output. Dynamic 4D scenes from text alone, in which liquids flow, particles emit, rigid bodies cascade, and articulated mechanisms move, remain largely unexplored despite their value as editable content and as physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. Two challenges set the dynamic case apart from static text-to-scene work: an agent must jointly coordinate spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting in a single coherent scene, and verifying motion correctness from rendered video is fundamentally harder than judging a single image. We present SimWorlds: a multi-agent framework that produces dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text, with Blender-specific procedural knowledge, a planner-coder-reviewer workflow driving a fixed ordered sequence of construction stages, a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier, and a runtime-state inspection tool suite that catches mechanism failures the rendered image cannot reveal. We also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark for assessing both visual fidelity and physical consistency of the procedural dynamic 3D scenes generated from text prompts. Experiments show that SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines.

AI.tldr: SimWorlds is a multi-agent framework that generates dynamic, editable 4D scenes from text by coordinating spatial layout, physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting, using a planner-coder-reviewer workflow and runtime-state inspection tools. It also introduces 4DBuildBench for evaluating visual fidelity and physical consistency. Experiments show it outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based systems for translating text into 3D scenes produce only static output, leaving dynamic 4D scenes (liquids, particles, rigid bodies, articulated mechanisms) unexplored. Such dynamic scenes are valuable as editable content and physics-grounded training data for video generation and embodied AI. Two key challenges exist: coordinating spatial layout, multiple physics solvers, temporal sequencing, camera, and lighting coherently; and verifying motion correctness from rendered video being fundamentally harder than judging a single image.
AI.method: SimWorlds is a multi-agent framework incorporating: (1) Blender-specific procedural knowledge; (2) a planner-coder-reviewer workflow driving a fixed ordered sequence of construction stages; (3) a layered scene protocol enforced by a deterministic verifier; and (4) a runtime-state inspection tool suite that catches mechanism failures not visible in rendered images.
AI.result: SimWorlds outperforms prior dynamic Blender generation baselines. The authors also introduce 4DBuildBench, a benchmark for assessing both visual fidelity and physical consistency of procedural dynamic 3D scenes generated from text prompts.
AI.conclusion: SimWorlds addresses the challenges of generating dynamic 4D scenes from text by using a multi-agent framework with structured workflows, deterministic verification, and runtime inspection, demonstrating superior performance over existing baselines.

title: Episodic-to-Semantic Consolidation Without Identity Drift
summary: Long-running adaptive intelligent agents face a structural tension between knowledge consolidation and information integrity. Memory consolidation is conventionally treated as an agent-changing operation: a model is fine-tuned, a prompt rewritten, a policy distilled, or a reflection appended to the context that governs future behaviour. In regulated autonomic deployment this is a liability because the agent operates under commitments and audit contracts that bind to a specific, cryptographically certified identity. We propose to treat consolidation not as a mutation of the planner or the identity manifest, but as a deterministic function f: M^ep -> M^sem over episodic memory whose output is a separately addressable semantic knowledge layer; the identity hash does not read M^sem, so consolidation updates knowledge without changing the agent's certified identity. We give a formal account of the agent representation, prove identity invariance through a structural lemma on the manifest's hash-input set, specify a deterministic aggregation algorithm whose outputs are auditable database rows with explicit confidence and supporting-event provenance, and validate the construction with synthetic experiments demonstrating per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, and a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%] across 10 seeds) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline. The construction is a knowledge-update discipline for autonomic agents in which lessons accumulate as queryable facts while the agent's certified identity remains byte-equal across its operational lifetime, with an embodied service agent as the running case study.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes treating memory consolidation in autonomous agents as a deterministic function over episodic memory that produces a separate semantic knowledge layer, rather than modifying the agent's identity or planner. This preserves the agent's cryptographically certified identity while allowing knowledge updates, with formal proofs and experiments showing 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts.
AI.motivation: Long-running adaptive agents face a tension between knowledge consolidation (which conventionally mutates the agent) and information integrity (agents operate under audit contracts bound to a certified identity). Consolidation as a mutation is a liability in regulated autonomic deployment.
AI.method: Consolidation is formalized as a deterministic function f: M^ep -> M^sem that maps episodic memory to a separate, addressable semantic knowledge layer. The identity hash does not read M^sem, so the agent's certified identity remains unchanged. A deterministic aggregation algorithm with explicit confidence and provenance is specified, and identity invariance is proved via a structural lemma on the manifest's hash-input set.
AI.result: Synthetic experiments demonstrate per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, and a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%] across 10 seeds) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline.
AI.conclusion: The construction provides a knowledge-update discipline for autonomic agents where lessons accumulate as queryable facts while the agent's certified identity remains byte-equal across its operational lifetime, validated with an embodied service agent case study.

title: Repair the Amplifier, Not the Symptom: Stable World-Model Correction for Agent Rollouts
summary: As agent planning moves from short tool chains toward persistent workflows with thousands or tens of thousands of steps, failures will occur inside large planning graphs rather than in isolated predictions. Replanning the entire graph after every mistake is neither computationally realistic nor desirable: full-graph replay consumes large context budgets, exposes the LLM to many irrelevant symptoms, and can degrade long-context retrieval. This paper studies the missing component in such systems: a world-model corrector that repairs the failed planning graph in place. We compare two families of correctors. The first is the common engineering approach: scan nodes and edges, choose a suspicious local region, and ask an LLM to repair it. We implement strong engineering LLM correctors and find that they can help, especially when given very large contexts. The second family is our approach, WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair): instead of scanning for visible symptoms, it works backward from subgraph amplification, identifies the nodes and edges that keep re-amplifying error, and sends only that causal subgraph to the LLM. Across graph simulations and LLM repair experiments, WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact region, and gives the LLM a cleaner repair target.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces WM-SAR, a world-model corrector that repairs failed planning graphs by identifying causal error subgraphs, outperforming engineering-based LLM correctors under realistic token budgets.
AI.motivation: As agent planning scales to long workflows with thousands of steps, replanning entire graphs after every failure is computationally infeasible and degrades performance. A targeted repair mechanism for failed planning graphs is missing.
AI.method: Proposes WM-SAR (World-Model Subgraph Amplification Repair), which works backward from subgraph amplification to identify nodes/edges that re-amplify errors, sending only that causal subgraph to the LLM for repair. Compared against engineering LLM correctors that scan and repair suspicious local regions.
AI.result: WM-SAR substantially outperforms engineering correctors under realistic token budgets, achieves near-whole-graph stabilization with a compact region, and provides cleaner repair targets to the LLM.
AI.conclusion: Causal subgraph repair is more effective than symptom-scanning approaches for fixing persistent planning graph failures under constrained computational budgets.

title: Verifiable Knowledge Expansion through Retrieval-Grounded Formal Concept Analysis
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures, Accepted to the 8th epiDAMIK ACM SIGKDD International Workshop on Epidemiology meets Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery (epiDAMIK 2026)
summary: Ontology construction requires deciding which objects, attributes, and structural relations should be accepted as valid knowledge. Language models can propose such structures from text, but their outputs can still be unsupported or inconsistent. This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework that uses formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop for knowledge expansion. Starting from seed attributes, FCA proposes implications over a growing formal context. A retrieval-grounded SLM oracle then validates each implication or returns a counterexample. The oracle also supports incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals, making accepted implications, counterexamples, contradictions, and corrections inspectable. In a rare ataxia setting constructed from Orphadata resources, retrieval-grounded 10-seed runs obtain relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22-0.30. Larger seed sets increase the number of evaluated implications and often improve implication F1. The lower implication scores reflect a stricter evaluation of derived implications, where one missed or extra relation can affect several implication judgments. Ablations show that incidence judgments in a fixed object-attribute setting can improve closure-based implication scores. However, identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult even when the candidate objects and attributes are fixed.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a retrieval-augmented small language model (SLM) framework with formal concept analysis (FCA) as a symbolic verification loop for ontology construction from text, evaluated on rare ataxia data.
AI.motivation: Ontology construction requires deciding valid objects, attributes, and structural relations; language models can propose such structures from text but often produce unsupported or inconsistent outputs.
AI.method: A retrieval-augmented SLM oracle validates FCA-proposed implications over a growing formal context, supporting incidence judgments, consistency checks, and attribute proposals.
AI.result: Relation F1 of 0.29-0.52 and closure-based implication F1 of 0.22-0.30 in rare ataxia setting; larger seed sets improve implication F1; incidence judgments improve closure-based scores but identifying positive object-attribute pairs remains difficult.
AI.conclusion: The FCA-SLM framework enables inspectable knowledge expansion, though derived implication evaluation is strict and object-attribute identification remains challenging.

title: Subliminal Clocks: Latent Time Modelling in Diffusion Language Models
comment: Equal contribution: Thomas Fontanari and Simone Petruzzi
summary: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive models. Unlike standard diffusion-based approaches, DLMs are not explicitly conditioned on a timestep, raising a natural question: do these models internally represent denoising progress, and how is such information used downstream? In this work, we show that DLMs do in fact encode a latent representation related to the diffusion timestep within their residual streams. We find that this signal can be reliably extracted using probes across layers, indicating that denoising progress is decodable from internal activations. We further demonstrate that steering the model along a low-dimensional subspace associated with the inferred timestep allows us to systematically modulate its notion of denoising progress, leading to predictable changes in model confidence and entropy. Finally, we analyse the geometry of the identified representation, showing that it exhibits structured and interpretable properties in activation space, and shedding light on how such a signal is processed by these models.

AI.tldr: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) encode an internal representation of denoising progress (timestep) in their residual streams, which can be extracted via probes, steered to modulate confidence/entropy, and exhibits structured activation geometry.
AI.motivation: DLMs operate without explicit timestep conditioning, unlike standard diffusion models. The authors investigate whether these models internally represent denoising progress and how such information is used downstream.
AI.method: The authors probe internal activations across layers to decode timestep information, steer the model along a low-dimensional subspace associated with inferred timestep to modulate denoising progress, and analyze the geometric properties of the identified representation.
AI.result: DLMs encode a latent representation of the diffusion timestep decodable from internal activations. Steering along the inferred timestep subspace systematically changes model confidence and entropy. The representation exhibits structured and interpretable properties in activation space.
AI.conclusion: Despite lacking explicit timestep conditioning, DLMs internally track denoising progress, and this signal can be extracted and manipulated, offering insights into how these models process information.

title: Safety Testing LLM Agents at Scale: From Risk Discovery to Evidence-Grounded Verification
summary: LLM agents increasingly perform autonomous actions through external tools, leading to complex and evolving safety risks. However, existing safety testing targets expert-designed safety violations, and the corresponding outcomes are evaluated by hard-coded rules, making them costly to extend as agents evolve. To this end, we present Vera, an end-to-end automated safety testing framework that instantiates software engineering testing principles for non-deterministic agents through a three-stage, self-reinforcing pipeline. First, a literature-driven exploration continuously discovers and structures emerging risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments. Second, combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions produces executable safety cases, each specifying a concrete safety goal, a programmatically constructed initial state, and a deterministic verification predicate grounded in observable artifacts. Third, adaptive execution runs heterogeneous agents in isolated sandboxes where a control agent steers multi-turn interaction based on runtime observations, while evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence rather than model self-report. We evaluate Vera on four production agent frameworks (OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, Claude Code), revealing substantial safety weaknesses, with average attack success rates reaching 93.9\% under multi-channel attacks; we also release Vera-Bench, comprising 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings. These results indicate that modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/Yunhao-Feng/Vera.

AI.tldr: Vera is an end-to-end automated safety testing framework for LLM agents that uses a three-stage pipeline (literature-driven risk exploration, combinatorial safety case composition, and adaptive execution with evidence-grounded verification) to systematically discover and test safety vulnerabilities. Evaluated on four production agent frameworks, it reveals 93.9% average attack success rates under multi-channel attacks and releases Vera-Bench with 1600 executable safety cases across 124 risk categories.
AI.motivation: Existing safety testing for LLM agents relies on expert-designed safety violations and hard-coded rules, making them costly and difficult to extend as agents evolve rapidly. There is a need for an automated, scalable, and maintainable approach to discover and test emerging safety risks in autonomous agent systems.
AI.method: Three-stage self-reinforcing pipeline: (1) literature-driven exploration that continuously discovers and structures emerging risks into taxonomies of safety risks, attack methods, and tool execution environments; (2) combinatorial composition across taxonomy dimensions to produce executable safety cases with concrete safety goals, programmatically constructed initial states, and deterministic verification predicates; (3) adaptive execution where a control agent steers multi-turn interactions in isolated sandboxes and evidence-grounded verifiers judge outcomes from environment state and tool-call evidence.
AI.result: Evaluated on OpenClaw, Hermes, Codex, and Claude Code frameworks. Average attack success rates reached 93.9% under multi-channel attacks. Released Vera-Bench with 1600 executable safety cases spanning 124 risk categories across three execution settings.
AI.conclusion: Modular, executable testing infrastructure is essential for rigorous and maintainable safety evaluation of rapidly evolving agentic systems at scale.

title: MMIR-TCM: Memory-Integrated Multimodal Inference and Retrieval for TCM Clinical Decision Support
summary: Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) diagnosis, particularly through tongue inspection, faces persistent challenges in subjectivity and reproducibility. The application of multimodal artificial intelligence to TCM clinical tasks, such as syndrome differentiation and prescription generation, is significantly hampered by the semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, as well as the lack of large-scale, standardized datasets. To address these challenges, we introduce MMIR-TCM, a novel framework that emulates the diagnostic process of TCM experts by integrating multimodal large language model(MLLM) with memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Employing a three-stage architecture, MMIR-TCM integrates a training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction, a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model for structured tongue diagnosis generation, and a Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support generation. The framework was developed and validated using MedTCM, a new large-scale multimodal dataset that we introduce specifically for advanced TCM research. To properly evaluate our framework's clinical accuracy, which existing metrics fail to capture, we also developed TDEU, a domain-specific evaluation metric incorporating semantic understanding and diagnostic importance. Our comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.

AI.tldr: MMIR-TCM is a multimodal AI framework for TCM tongue diagnosis that integrates Memory-SAM for tongue extraction, fine-tuned Qwen3-VL for structured diagnosis, and RAG for evidence-grounded clinical decisions. It introduces the MedTCM dataset and TDEU evaluation metric, outperforming GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash.
AI.motivation: TCM tongue diagnosis suffers from subjectivity and reproducibility issues. The semantic gap between visual tongue features and textual reasoning, along with the lack of large-scale standardized datasets, hinders multimodal AI applications for syndrome differentiation and prescription generation.
AI.method: Three-stage architecture: (1) training-free Memory-SAM module for robust tongue extraction; (2) fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model for structured tongue diagnosis generation; (3) Qwen3-based RAG component for evidence-grounded clinical decision support. Validated on the new MedTCM dataset and evaluated with the TDEU metric.
AI.result: MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash on comprehensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively bridges the semantic gap between visual and textual modalities in TCM, demonstrating superior clinical accuracy and providing a reproducible, explainable approach to AI-assisted TCM diagnosis.

title: Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Benchmark available in inspect_evals (UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_evals)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

AI.tldr: Pre-Flight is an open-source benchmark of 300 aviation-specific multiple-choice questions used to evaluate LLMs, revealing that even the strongest model (82.7% accuracy) falls short of expert-level performance (~95%), highlighting a persistent gap for safe deployment in aviation operations.
AI.motivation: General-purpose benchmarks fail to measure whether LLMs reason safely and correctly about aviation-specific operational knowledge, a high-stakes regulated domain where such gaps have serious consequences.
AI.method: The authors created 300 multiple-choice questions drawn from international standards (ICAO, FAA), airport ground operations, and complex operational scenarios, authored and reviewed by aviation practitioners. They evaluated commercial and open-weight models using the Inspect framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple-choice protocol.
AI.result: The strongest model (released in 2026) achieved 82.7% accuracy, improving from ~75% in early 2025, but still well below the informal expert reference of ~95% from aviation professionals, indicating a substantial and persistent reliability gap.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non-safety-critical aviation operations, and current models remain insufficiently reliable for such use.

title: Actual causality in fault trees
summary: Fault trees are a widely used as effective risk models for complex systems, answering the question "what can go wrong?", especially through minimal cut set analysis. We study fault trees from the perspective of Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality. This allows us to use fault trees to answer the question "why has it gone wrong?", which is fundamental to failure diagnostics. We give a complete classification of each of the different notions of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure, and show how minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges fault tree analysis (used for risk assessment) with Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality, enabling fault trees to answer not just "what can go wrong?" but also "why has it gone wrong?" for failure diagnostics. It classifies actual causality notions in terms of fault tree structure and shows how minimal cut sets correspond to actual causes.
AI.motivation: To extend fault tree analysis beyond risk assessment (what can go wrong) to failure diagnostics (why it has gone wrong) by incorporating actual causality theory.
AI.method: The paper provides a complete classification of Halpern & Pearl's actual causality notions in terms of fault tree graph structure and logical structure, and demonstrates the relationship between minimal cut sets and actual causes.
AI.result: The different notions of actual causality are fully classified with respect to fault tree structure, and minimal cut sets are shown to give rise to actual causes.
AI.conclusion: Fault trees can be effectively used for failure diagnostics by leveraging actual causality theory, with minimal cut sets serving as a bridge to identify actual causes of failures.

title: CLAP: Closed-Loop Training, Evaluation, and Release Control for Domain Agent Post-training
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to CRAE 2026; to appear in SPIE Proceedings. Best Poster Award
summary: Domain agents often face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk.
